A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Wan-based RGB-A video-generation project despite retitling and substantial revisions. All pages, figures, tables and equations support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix; v3 references separate supplementary material that is not included.

before.justification: v1 reports original generated-video comparisons, inference timings and failure examples in Sections 3.2–3.4 and Figures 10–20.

after.justification: v3 reports original quantitative comparisons, user rankings and reconstruction ablations in Tables 1–3, alongside transparency-control and image-to-video demonstrations.

M1.justification: v3 adds a transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion loss using a frozen DiT during VAE training, beyond v1's reconstruction objectives. It also introduces alpha-derived Gaussian ellipse masks that shift noise means during training and inference, enabling spatial transparency control. These change the objectives and generation procedure while retaining the shared-latent VAE and LoRA/DoRA framework.

E1.justification: The underlying matting datasets and Internet-data domains remain. However, v3 adds mask-conditioned generation with controllable subject position and size, and trains Wan2.1-I2V-14B for image-and-text-conditioned animation (Section 4.4; Figures 9–10). These extend v1's text-to-video task requirements. Changes in training sample counts are settings changes, not new dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates TransPixeler's open and closed versions. v3 retains both and adds LayerFlow (Single) and LayerDiffuse + AnimateDiff to the comparisons in Figure 5 and Tables 1–2. Figure 6 additionally evaluates Wan + MatAnyone, introducing a generation-plus-matting alternative.

E3.justification: v3 introduces white-background evaluation with VBench and GPT-4o metrics, user-ranking evaluation, and PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS reconstruction tests. Reported VAE/DiT training budgets change from 60,000/1,500 to 75,000/1,750 iterations. The generation-training collection changes from 437 to 429 samples: images increase from 20 to 43, Internet-effects videos decrease from 116 to 85, and matting videos remain 301.

E4.justification: v1 provides illustrative failures but no component ablations. v3 adds reconstruction ablations for rendering and the bidirectional loss (Table 3), generation ablations for that loss and mean sampling (Figure 7), mean-shift sensitivity tests (Figure 8), and mask-geometry tests (Figure 9). The earlier astronaut and explosion failure examples are not retained.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v3's new scores and average user rankings are point estimates; they do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds the first quantitative comparison, user-ranking and reconstruction tables. Examples include text alignment 4.00 and aesthetics 0.649 in Table 1, transparency/overall ranks 1.23/1.11 in Table 2, and full-model RGB/alpha PSNR 41.47/42.22 in Table 3. Qualitative comparisons are replaced and control/animation findings added. These are newly reported results, not matched v1-to-v3 gains; the 128-second versus 32-minute timing comparison remains.

T1.justification: v3 introduces mathematical definitions for the signed transparency mask and bidirectional loss, conditional Gaussian noise, and covariance-based ellipse construction (Equations 1–3 and 12–19). No theorems or proofs are added. Equation 13 also writes the velocity target as Z_t minus shifted noise, unlike v1's noise minus Z; this is inconsistent with the stated interpolation.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on high-quality, efficient transparent generation through a shared-latent VAE and curated data. v3 redefines the central contribution as shifting alpha distributions while preserving RGB generation, explicitly claiming stable and spatially controllable transparency. These new mechanism and capability claims appear throughout the abstract, introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 attributes transparency holes to RGB–alpha entanglement and explains why preserving RGB capability can retain unwanted backgrounds without mean sampling. It adds qualifications about weak control at small mean shifts and red bias at large shifts. v1's broader discussion of remaining unnatural content, background debris and inaccurate masks is no longer retained as a limitations assessment.

D1.justification: v3 specifies the Wan2.1-T2V-14B backbone, its I2V counterpart, and a typical mean-shift strength of 0.05. It omits v1's 272 × 272, 17-frame crop specification, caption-language/manual-refinement details and testing-prompt instructions. Common adapter ranks, batch sizes and the project link remain. These omissions establish documentation changes, not changes to the underlying preprocessing.

R1.justification: v3 substantially repositions the work around distribution separation, criticizing prior methods for entangling RGB and alpha rather than primarily emphasizing quality and efficiency. It connects its sampler to BBDM, TKG-DM, ShiftDDPMs and Shifted Diffusion, and expands the comparison and evaluation literature with MatAnyone, VBench and OpenS2V.

P1.justification: v3 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, method narrative and conclusion. It creates a separate Related Work section, consolidates dataset discussion, compresses the reconstruction-loss exposition, and reorganizes experiments around comparisons, ablations and applications instead of v1's extended results gallery and limitations section.

P2.justification: The single-column presentation becomes a two-column layout. Framework diagrams are redrawn to include the new components, the detailed feature-merge diagram disappears, and several dataset illustrations are consolidated into Figure 4. Long comparison galleries are replaced by compact comparison panels, three quantitative tables, and new ablation, control and animation figures.

improvement.justification: v1's superiority claims rely mainly on selected visual examples and timing. v3 substantially strengthens their support through broader comparisons and component ablations, especially Table 3 and Figure 7. Material weaknesses remain: study sizes and uncertainty are unspecified, reproducibility details disappear, and Equation 13 is inconsistent. Table 2's transparency ranks also total 14 rather than the 15 expected for complete untied five-method rankings, without explanation. These issues limit confidence, but the controlled analyses provide a substantial net improvement in experimental support.
